title: A whole week
goal: Name the days, say how often you do things, and tell the time down to the minute.
bekal: name the days of the week

dialogs.title: Diálogo — La semana de Marta
dialogs.intro: Now it's Marta's turn to talk. Watch for the words that say how often.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What do you usually do on Mondays?

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Los lunes siempre trabajo en la librería.
lines.id: On Mondays I always work at the bookstore.
lines.literal: the Mondays always I-work in the bookstore.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Igual. Pero los jueves estudio inglés por la tarde.
lines.id: Same. But on Thursdays I study English in the afternoon.
lines.literal: same. but the Thursdays I-study English through the afternoon.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Sí, los fines de semana. Los sábados me levanto tarde.
lines.id: I do, on weekends. On Saturdays I get up late.
lines.literal: yes, the ends of week. the Saturdays I-raise-myself late.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: A las once, a veces a las doce. ¡Es mi lujo!
lines.id: At eleven, sometimes at twelve. It's my luxury!
lines.literal: at the hours eleven, at times at the hours twelve. is my-luxury!

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Los domingos comemos en casa de mis padres. Nunca falto.
lines.id: On Sundays we have lunch at my parents' house. I never miss it.
lines.literal: the Sundays we-eat in house of my-parents. never I-miss.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: ¡Qué bien! Nosotros también comemos juntos los domingos.
lines.id: How nice! We have lunch together on Sundays too.
lines.literal: how good! we also we-eat together the Sundays.

notes: **Nunca can double up with no.** *No descanso nunca* and *nunca descanso* are both correct and mean the same. Spanish allows stacked negatives — *no veo nada nunca* ("I don't never see nothing") is perfectly fine, something that's wrong in standard English.
**Sí as a contradiction.** When Marta answers *sí* to a negative question, it means "yes, I do!" — like English "I do" or French *si*. Spanish uses a stressed *sí*.

**Hacer** = to do / to make, one of the most common verbs. Its *yo* form is *hago*; the rest are regular: *haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen*. *¿Qué haces?* has two uses: "what are you doing?" and "what do you do (for a living)?"
**Comer has two meanings.** Generally "to eat", but in Spain *comer* specifically means to have lunch — the main meal of the day. Dinner is *cenar*, breakfast *desayunar*.
**Los fines de semana** — notice that it's *fin* that becomes plural, not *semana*: *los fines de semana*, not *los fin de semanas*. The same rule applies to every phrase joined with *de*.
**Igual** = "the same", a very common short answer. It also appears in *me da igual* ("it's all the same to me", "I don't mind").

**Normalmente, generalmente, tranquilamente.** Adverbs are formed from the feminine adjective + **-mente**: *normal → normalmente*, *rápida → rápidamente*, *tranquila → tranquilamente*. Just like the English ending -ly.
**Juntos / juntas** = together, and the form follows the group: *comemos juntos* (mixed or all male), *comemos juntas* (all female).

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The formula has two parts: **Es la una** for one o'clock, **Son las…** for every other hour. Minutes are added with *y* up to half past, then *menos* after that — Spanish counts back from the next hour.
after: To make morning or evening clear, add *de la mañana* (roughly 6 a.m.-12 noon), *de la tarde* (noon until dark), or *de la noche* (after dark). So *las ocho de la mañana* and *las ocho de la tarde* are two very different times.
Official schedules — stations, airports, cinemas — use the 24-hour clock as is: *el tren sale a las diecinueve treinta*. Everyday speech still uses the 12-hour system in this table.

blocks.text: Days are written in lowercase, and the first five already look plural: *el lunes* is one Monday, *los lunes* is every Monday. Only *sábado* and *domingo* change: *los sábados*, *los domingos*.

Meaning
Example

blocks.title: A day shifted by two hours
items: Spain's clock runs about two hours behind its European neighbors. Lunch is at 2 p.m., dinner at 9-10 p.m., and prime-time TV doesn't start until 10:30 p.m. A dinner invitation for 8 p.m. is a tourist's invitation.

*La siesta* does exist, but it isn't the national afternoon nap people imagine. What's real is the *horario partido* (split schedule): many small shops close from 2 to 5 p.m., then reopen until 8 p.m.
So don't be surprised if the pharmacy or post office is closed exactly when you're free. Big stores and shopping malls usually stay open all day.
In Latin America the pattern is much closer to North America: lunch around 12-1 p.m., dinner around 7-8 p.m.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of *ir* (*voy*, *vas*, *va*, *vamos*, *van*).
items: Marta ____ a la librería los lunes.
Normalmente me acuesto a las once.
Los domingos comemos en casa de mis padres.
A veces trabajo el sábado por la mañana.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a correct Spanish sentence.

answers: I usually go to bed at eleven. — On Sundays we have lunch at my parents' house. — I'm never late for work. — It takes me half an hour to get there. — Sometimes I work on Saturday morning.
¿Qué hora es? — Me levanto a las seis. — Los domingos descanso. — Nunca llego tarde. — Voy al trabajo en moto.
